title: Sweat: cooling by evaporation
goal: Explain how evaporating sweat removes heat, work out how much sweat a given heat load needs, and say why humid air, dripping sweat and large differences between athletes matter.

steps.title: Evaporation: the heat sink that always works
steps.text:
Turning liquid into vapour takes energy, the [latent heat of vaporisation](g:latent-heat). Each gram of sweat that evaporates from the skin takes **2,426 J** (about 2.4 kJ) with it [[c:sw-latent-heat]]. A litre evaporated removes about 2,400 kJ.

That makes [evaporation](g:evaporative-heat-loss) the main heat-loss route in warm and hot weather [[c:sw-main-route]]. It is also the only route that still works when air and sun are hotter than skin, because it doesn't need a temperature difference: it needs *dry enough air*.

The key word is *evaporates*. Sweat on the skin does nothing until it turns to vapour.

claims.text: Each gram of sweat evaporated from the skin removes 2,426 J of heat.

evidence.quote: Since the evaporation of 1 g of sweat off the skin liberates 2,426 J of latent heat energy ( 93 )

claims.text: Evaporative sweating is the main way the body loses heat in warm and hot environments.

evidence.quote: Evaporative sweating is the principal means of heat loss in warm-hot environments where sweat losses frequently exceed fluid intakes.

steps.title: How much sweat to lose 1,000 W?
steps.problem: From the last lesson: a rider at 250 W makes about 1,000 W of heat. On a hot day, suppose all of it must leave by evaporation. How much sweat must evaporate in 1 h?
steps: Heat to remove in 1 h: 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 J.
Common slip: forgetting the time and dividing 1,000 by 2,426 (0.41 g). Watts are joules *per second*.

steps.title: Dripping sweat doesn't cool
steps.text:
Sweat that drips off, or soaks into a jersey and stays there, takes almost no heat from the body. The share that evaporates is the [sweating efficiency](g:sweating-efficiency). It falls with **humid air, still air, high work rates and clothing** that blocks vapour [[c:sw-efficiency-falls]].

Humidity is the big one: evaporation needs a gap between the water vapour pressure at wet skin and in the air. Humid air narrows that gap, so you sweat more for the same cooling [[c:sw-humidity]].

Once about half the skin must be wet ([skin wettedness](g:skin-wettedness) above about 0.5), more sweat starts to drip and cooling per gram falls [[c:sw-wettedness]]. A drenched rider on a muggy turbo session is not cooling better; he is losing water for little cooling.

claims.text: Sweating efficiency falls at high absolute intensity, in humid or still air and with clothing of high evaporative resistance, because sweat drips or stays on the skin.

evidence.quote: When exercise is performed at a high absolute intensity, in a humid and/or still-air environment, and/or with clothing with a relatively high evaporative resistance, sweating efficiency declines.
That is, a proportion of secreted sweat does not evaporate from the skin but instead remains on the skin, drips off the body altogether, and/or becomes trapped in clothing.

claims.text: Above a required skin wettedness of about 0.50, the evaporative efficiency of sweat is reported to fall below 100%.

evidence.quote: a skin wettedness required for heat balance (ω req ) of 0.50, the critical value above which the evaporative efficiency of sweat is reported to decline from 100%.

claims.text: High humidity narrows the water vapour gradient, reduces evaporation and requires a higher sweat rate for the same cooling.

evidence.quote: ↓ Water vapor gradient leads to ↓ evaporation of sweat, which ↑ T c and the need for higher SR than calculated from E req , but prolonged exposure can lead to hidromeiosis and decreased SR

steps.title: How much do athletes sweat?
steps.text:
Sweat rate follows the **heat that must be lost by evaporation**, not the percentage of VO₂max: in a well-controlled study, the evaporative requirement explained almost all the differences in sweat rate [[c:sw-rate-ereq]]. More watts, hotter air, more sun: more sweat.

Athletes typically sweat about **0.5–2.0 L·h⁻¹**; above 3.0 L·h⁻¹ is rare [[c:sw-rate-range]] (most of these data come from a sports-drink company's lab: see below).

You can measure your own: weigh yourself, nude and dry, before and after a session. Add what you drank; 1 kg lost is about 1 L of sweat. That is the simplest accurate method [[c:sw-mass-method]], within small errors from urine and breathing.

claims.text: Whole-body sweat rate is determined by the evaporative requirement for heat balance, not by relative exercise intensity.

evidence.quote: These data provide clear evidence that absolute WBSR during exercise is determined by Ereq, not by % .
In conclusion, changes in core temperature and sweating during exercise in a neutral climate are determined by H(prod), mass, and BSA, not Vo(₂ peak).

claims.text: Athletes' whole-body sweat rate typically ranges from about 0.5 to 2.0 L per hour; above 3.0 L per hour is rare.

evidence.quote: As this and other studies have shown, WBSR typically ranges from approximately 0.5 to approximately 2.0 L/h [ 2 , 24 , 96 ].
WBSR can be >3.0 L/h [ 9 , 15 , 96 , 137 – 141 ] but this is relatively rare (approximately 2% of athletes in Fig. 1 a)

claims.text: Change in body mass during exercise is the simplest and most accurate way to measure whole-body sweat rate.

evidence.quote: The simplest and most accurate method to assess whole-body SR is via changes in body mass during exercise; however, potential confounding factors to consider are non-sweat sources of mass change and trapped sweat in clothing.

steps.title: Sweat rate from the scales
steps.problem: A runner weighs 70.0 kg before a 90 min run and 68.6 kg after. She drank 0.5 L during it. What was her sweat rate?
steps: Add what she drank, which she also sweated out: 1.4 + 0.5 = 1.9 L.
Divide by time in hours: 1.9 L ÷ 1.5 h = 1.27 L·h⁻¹ (ignoring urine and breathing losses).

steps.title: What is in sweat: sodium
steps.text:
Sweat starts in the glands as a fluid like plasma (about 135–145 mmol·L⁻¹ of sodium), but the ducts take much of the sodium back before it reaches the skin [[c:sw-duct-reabsorb]]. What arrives is **saltier in some people than others**: about 10–90 mmol·L⁻¹ measured at one patch of skin, about 10–70 mmol·L⁻¹ for the whole body [[c:sw-sodium-range]].

So two triathletes sweating 1.5 L·h⁻¹ can lose very different amounts of salt. White salt stains on a kit hint at a salty sweater, but only a proper sweat test tells you.

Much of the sweat-testing data come from one sports-drink company's institute; the method is sound, but keep the source in mind.

claims.text: Local sweat sodium typically ranges from about 10 to 90 mmol per litre, and whole-body sweat sodium from about 10 to 70 mmol per litre.

evidence.quote: Local sweat [Na + ] typically ranges from approximately 10 to approximately 90 mmol/L (Fig.
while whole-body sweat [Na + ] is approximately 10–70 mmol/L (predicted, Fig.

claims.text: Primary sweat is nearly isotonic with plasma; sodium is reabsorbed as sweat flows through the duct.

evidence.quote: Primary sweat is nearly isotonic with blood plasma (e.g. approximately 135–145 mmol/L Na + , approximately 95–110 mmol/L Cl − , and approximately 4–5 mmol/L K + ) [ 29 , 46 – 49 ].
As sweat flows through the duct, Na + is passively reabsorbed via epithelial Na + channels (ENaCs) on the luminal membrane

points: Each gram of sweat that evaporates removes 2,426 J: a litre evaporated takes about 2,400 kJ of heat.
Evaporation is the main heat sink in the heat, and the only one when air and sun are hotter than skin.
Dripping or trapped sweat cools almost nothing; humid or still air and clothing cut sweating efficiency.
Sweat rate follows the heat that must be lost by evaporation; athletes typically sweat 0.5–2.0 L·h⁻¹. Measure it with the scales: mass lost plus fluid drunk, per hour.
Sweat sodium varies about 10–90 mmol·L⁻¹ between people, so salt losses differ widely at the same sweat rate.

variants.stem: About how much heat does 1 g of sweat remove from the body when it evaporates?

options.why: Right: the latent heat of vaporisation of sweat is 2,426 J per gram.
That is roughly the heat to warm 1 g of water by 1 °C; turning it to vapour takes about 580 times more.
Ten times too much: it is about 2.4 kJ per gram, so 2,400 kJ per litre.
Ten times too little: it is about 2.4 kJ per gram.

variants.stem: A rider's sweat evaporates completely. Roughly how much heat does 1 L (1,000 g) of it remove?

options.why: Ten times too little: each gram removes about 2.4 kJ, not 0.24 kJ.
That is about what warms 1 g of water by 1 °C; evaporation takes far more energy.
Ten times too much: 1,000 g × 2.4 kJ = 2,400 kJ.

variants.stem: A runner must lose 800 W of heat by evaporation for 1 h. How much sweat must evaporate? (2,426 J per gram)

options.why: This divides 800 by 2,426 and forgets the time. Watts are joules per second: multiply by 3,600 s.
This multiplies by 60 minutes instead of 3,600 seconds.
This assumes 1 g removes 1 kJ. Each gram removes 2.426 kJ: divide 2,880 kJ by 2.426.

variants.stem: A cyclist must lose 600 W of heat by evaporation for 1 h. How much sweat must evaporate? (2,426 J per gram)

options.why: This divides 600 by 2,426 and forgets the time. Watts are joules per second: multiply by 3,600 s.
This multiplies by 60 minutes instead of 3,600 seconds.
This assumes 1 g removes 1 kJ. Each gram removes 2.426 kJ: divide 2,160 kJ by 2.426.

variants.stem: In a 90 min half-Ironman run, a triathlete must lose 700 W of heat by evaporation. How much sweat must evaporate? (2,426 J per gram)

options.why: This divides 700 by 2,426 and forgets the time. Watts are joules per second: multiply by 5,400 s.
This multiplies by 90 minutes instead of 5,400 seconds.
This assumes 1 g removes 1 kJ. Each gram removes 2.426 kJ: divide 3,780 kJ by 2.426.

variants.stem: On an indoor trainer with no fan, sweat pours off a rider onto the floor. How much does that dripping sweat cool him?

options.text: Almost not at all: only sweat that evaporates from the skin removes heat
options.why: Right: the latent heat is taken only when sweat turns to vapour on the skin.

options.text: A lot: more sweat on the floor means more heat lost
options.why: Volume lost is not heat lost. Dripping sweat leaves as liquid and takes almost no heat.

options.text: The same 2.4 kJ per gram as evaporated sweat
options.why: The 2.4 kJ·g⁻¹ is paid only for evaporation; dripping sweat carries just a little warmth.

options.text: Half as much as evaporated sweat, as it evaporates on the floor
options.why: Evaporating on the floor takes heat from the floor, not from the rider.

variants.stem: Same 10 km pace, same 31 °C: one race is in dry desert air, one in muggy coastal air at 85% humidity. Why is the coastal race harder to keep cool in?

options.text: Humid air slows evaporation, so more sweat drips and less heat leaves
options.why: Right: a smaller vapour-pressure gap cuts evaporation and sweating efficiency.

options.text: Humid air is hotter than dry air at the same reading
options.why: Both are 31 °C. Humidity doesn't change the air temperature; it limits evaporation.

options.text: Humid air stops the body from producing sweat
options.why: Sweating goes on, often heavily; the problem is that less of it evaporates.

options.text: Humid air blocks convection from the skin
options.why: Convection depends on air temperature and speed, which are the same here.

variants.stem: A rider needs 1.2 L of sweat to evaporate in an hour, but in humid air only 70% of what he sweats evaporates. How much must he sweat?

options.why: Right: 1.2 ÷ 0.70 = 1.71 L; the extra 0.5 L drips or soaks in.
This multiplies by 0.70. If only 70% evaporates, he must sweat *more* than 1.2 L, not less.
This assumes all sweat evaporates. Here 30% is wasted, so he must sweat more.
This adds 30% of 1.2 L (1.2 × 1.3). The 1.2 L must be 70% of the total: divide by 0.70.

variants.solution: Sweat needed = evaporation needed ÷ sweating efficiency = 1.2 L ÷ 0.70 = 1.71 L.

variants.stem: A runner needs 0.9 L of sweat to evaporate in an hour; in still, humid air only 60% of her sweat evaporates. How much must she sweat?

options.why: Right: 0.9 ÷ 0.60 = 1.5 L; 0.6 L drips or stays on the skin.
This multiplies by 0.60. If only 60% evaporates, she must sweat *more* than 0.9 L, not less.
This assumes all sweat evaporates. Here 40% is wasted, so she must sweat more.
This adds 40% of 0.9 L (0.9 × 1.4). The 0.9 L must be 60% of the total: divide by 0.60.

variants.solution: Sweat needed = evaporation needed ÷ sweating efficiency = 0.9 L ÷ 0.60 = 1.5 L.

variants.stem: A runner weighs 70.0 kg before a 90 min run and 68.6 kg after; she drank 0.5 L. What was her sweat rate?

options.why: This forgets the 0.5 L she drank, which she also sweated out.
This subtracts the drink instead of adding it.
That is the total sweat loss; divide by 1.5 h to get a rate per hour.

variants.solution: Mass lost 1.4 kg ≈ 1.4 L. Sweat = 1.4 + 0.5 = 1.9 L. Rate = 1.9 ÷ 1.5 h = 1.27 L·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A cyclist weighs 64.0 kg before a 45 min turbo session and 62.8 kg after; he drank 0.6 L. What was his sweat rate?

options.why: This forgets the 0.6 L he drank, which he also sweated out.
This subtracts the drink instead of adding it.
That is the total sweat loss in 45 min; divide by 0.75 h to get a rate per hour.

variants.solution: Mass lost 1.2 kg ≈ 1.2 L. Sweat = 1.2 + 0.6 = 1.8 L. Rate = 1.8 ÷ 0.75 h = 2.4 L·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete weighs 80.0 kg before a 2 h brick session and 78.2 kg after; she drank 1.0 L. What was her sweat rate?

options.why: This forgets the 1.0 L she drank, which she also sweated out.
This subtracts the drink instead of adding it.
That is the total sweat loss over 2 h; divide by 2 to get a rate per hour.

variants.solution: Mass lost 1.8 kg ≈ 1.8 L. Sweat = 1.8 + 1.0 = 2.8 L. Rate = 2.8 ÷ 2 h = 1.4 L·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A fit and a less fit cyclist of the same size ride side by side at the same 220 W in the same weather. The fit one is at 45% of VO₂max, the other at 65%. How do their sweat rates compare, roughly?

options.text: Similar, because they make about the same heat that must be lost
options.why: Right: same watts and size give the same heat production and evaporative requirement, which sets sweat rate.

options.text: Higher in the less fit rider, because he is at a higher % of VO₂max
options.why: Sweat rate follows the heat to be lost, not the % of VO₂max.

options.text: Higher in the fit rider, because training makes everyone sweat more
options.why: Training can shift sweating a little, but at the same heat load the requirement, and so the rate, is about the same.

options.text: It can't be said without their heart rates
options.why: Heart rate doesn't set sweat rate; the heat to be lost by evaporation does.

variants.stem: Two triathletes both sweat 1.5 L·h⁻¹. A coach gives them the same salt plan, based on an average sweat sodium. How good is that plan?

options.text: Weak: sweat sodium varies several-fold between people
options.why: Right: about 10–90 mmol·L⁻¹ locally, so the same sweat rate can mean very different sodium losses.

options.text: Good: the same sweat rate means the same salt loss
options.why: Sodium loss = sweat volume × sodium concentration, and the concentration varies widely.

options.text: Good: sweat is about as salty as blood plasma
options.why: Sweat ducts reabsorb sodium, so sweat is much less salty than plasma (about 135–145 mmol·L⁻¹).

options.text: Weak: sweat holds no sodium worth replacing
options.why: Sweat sodium is real and varies; in long races losses can be large for salty sweaters.

variants.stem: A review of sweat rate and sodium uses data from about 500 athletes tested by a sports-drink company's institute, where the author works. What is the most sensible way to read it?

options.text: Use the data, but check its claims against independent studies
options.why: Right: funding doesn't make data wrong, but it raises the risk of biased framing, so look for independent support.

options.text: Set it aside: industry-funded work can't be relied on
options.why: Funding is a reason for care, not proof of error. Methods and independent replication decide.

options.text: Accept it as it is: it passed peer review
options.why: Peer review doesn't remove conflicts of interest; it is a check, not a guarantee.

options.text: Accept it as it is: 500 athletes is a large sample
options.why: A large sample cuts random error, not bias from who chose and framed the data.
